title: It's Blogging Time
---
<p><img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="">  </p>
<p>I’ve been posting a weekly recap on Instagram for the past 4 years of my life. This has been <em>tremendously valuable</em> for me. Initially I did it to rewire my relationship with posting, but it evolved into a meaningful part of my life.  </p>
<p>After having a few comics get 1000+ likes, I had an appetite {% 'appetite' 'I was never a real junkie but it was enough to form a habit' %} for that kind of attention. After posting something I’d check my notifications every 10 minutes for the next 3-7 days. I hated this.  </p>
<p>At the time I had a languishing personal Instagram that I never posted on because nothing seemed important enough to post. I decided to solve these problems with the same solution: I would private the instagram, remove anyone I wanted to impress {% 'impress' 'Steve Anderson, the director of <em>Meet The Robinson’s,</em> was following me? Which was lovely (he’s a lovely man) but did make me overthink posting' %} and start posting again. The big rules were that 1) I would post weekly and 2) not care how many likes I got.  </p>
<p>That was January of 2021. now, four years later, I want to wind down my habit and switch it out for a new one. I’ll give some general reflections, and then explain why I’m going to migrate to blogging.  </p>
<h3>Reflections on the weekly insta posts:</h3>
<ul>
<li>The fixed time duration ended up being surprisingly meaningful. The week I graduated college, the week my dog died, and the week Donald Trump was re-elected on my dead mother’s birthday held the same posting-weight as the weeks I debugged code, the weeks I went to a play with my girlfriend, {% 'girlfriend' 'Hi Michelle! ❤️'%} or the weeks I did nothing at all. This has a controlling effect- the “unimportant” weeks get their due, and the “important” weeks lose some status.</li>
<li>I’ve gotten more compliments about my weekly posts than almost anything else I’ve done. Somewhere between 5-10 people in real life have randomly told me that they love these posts. This makes me feel warm and fuzzy.</li>
<li>In order to fill the posts, I take more photos and do more things. Even informally reflecting on how I spend my time has made me spend it better.</li>
</ul>
<h3>So why am I stopping?</h3>
<p>There’s a couple reasons:</p>
<ul>
<li>Meta is already evil and they’re only going to get worse</li>
<li>I’m spending too much time on Instagram Reels</li>
<li>I want to stop complaining about social media being bad, and start doing <em>something</em>.</li>
</ul>
<p>So: blogging. I won’t bore you with the hows but this is a blog hosted on a raspberry pi that I own. You’re viewing an HTML file on a computer in my apartment. There’s no chance of an maga-fied tech CEO making me feel weird about this.  </p>
<h3>The plan going forward:</h3>
<p>I’m going to start posting my weekly recaps on here. They will be much shorter than this post, usually just a few images and a paragraph. I want this to be easy. Eventually, I’ll incorporate a newsletter feature and announce this blog on Instagram. After enough essential people have rolled over, I’ll stop posting.  </p>
<p>I expect this to take 2-4 months. I don’t want to do this quickly, I don’t want to make a stink about leaving social media then just come back. I want this to feel considered, because it is.  </p>
<p>If we want to have an Internet that isn’t dependent on big platforms, that needs to start with us. Which has to include things like personal posts.  </p>
<p>Meta talks about it themselves: the core product they’re selling is connecting you with your friends and family. I think that I can be connected to my loved ones without Zuck and his algorithms and his ads mediating the process. This blog project, if successful, will prove that.  </p>
<p>love yah,<br>Ryan  </p>
